note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: a path or pattern has at most 8 segments
literal segments are 1 to 10 characters from a-z and 0-9; a pattern segment may also be "*"
handler names are 1 to 20 characters: a letter followed by letters, digits or "_"
clarifyingQuestions: How are ties between patterns with the same number of wildcards broken?
Does registering the same pattern again replace the handler?
Does "*" match exactly one segment, or also zero or several?
hints: A matching pattern has the same number of segments as the path, so think of patterns as words over segments.
Store patterns in a trie keyed by segment, with "*" as one more child; a query only follows the literal child equal to its segment and the "*" child.

Visit the literal child first and track the wildcard count; the first match found with the smallest count is the left-to-right most specific one, and any branch whose count already exceeds the best can be skipped.
invariants: every trie node at depth d corresponds to one pattern prefix of d segments
a candidate match visited earlier in literal-first order wins ties on wildcard count
chooseWhen: Routing and pattern dispatch with single-segment wildcards
tradeoffs: A trie shares prefixes and avoids scanning every route; a full scan is simpler and fine for few routes
hack2hire:68fa7c5e0fa32e4d82f4fc1f.variantLabel: Single variant: most specific wildcard route per path

clarifyingQuestions: Is k counted over adjacent pairs of the chosen subsequence only?
Can the subsequence be empty?
How large can k be compared with the length?
hints: Taking an element never hurts except through the change budget; the question is only where the last chosen element came from.
For each value v and budget j, remember the longest subsequence that ends with v and uses j changes.
An element x either continues its own value at the same budget or follows the best subsequence of any value at budget j - 1; keep a running best per budget and update budgets downwards.
invariants: best[v][j] never decreases as more elements are read
top[j] equals the maximum of best[v][j] over all values seen so far
chooseWhen: Subsequence problems with a budget on value changes
tradeoffs: Keying the state by value avoids the quadratic scan over predecessors; the index-pair programme is simpler but O(n^2 k)
hack2hire:686b0a7af56e0403f35f23ee.variantLabel: Single variant: longest subsequence with at most k value changes

clarifyingQuestions: Is there a "?" wildcard as well?
Must the whole of s be matched?
Can consecutive "*" appear?
hints: Consecutive stars behave like one star.
Between two stars sits a literal piece that must appear somewhere in order.
Placing each middle piece at its leftmost possible position never hurts; only the first piece is anchored at the start and the last at the end.
invariants: pieces are placed in order without overlap
the prefix and suffix anchors do not overlap
tradeoffs: Piece-by-piece search uses fast substring search; the DP table is simpler to prove but quadratic in time and space

constraints: total characters in words at most 2e5
clarifyingQuestions: Is the mapping per character or per word?
Does a word of a different length simply fail?
Should the output be booleans or the matching words?
hints: A length mismatch fails immediately.
Two maps catch both directions of a conflict: one pattern character to two letters, or two pattern characters to one letter.
Equivalently, compare the first-occurrence index of every character in the pattern and in the word.
invariants: each map stays injective while scanning
positions scanned so far are consistent with one bijection
tradeoffs: Two maps per word are linear; precomputing the pattern's first-occurrence signature lets each word be checked with one map
hack2hire:67e45b2850b60b77022f382e.variantLabel: Single variant: character-level pattern bijection for many words

clarifyingQuestions: Are blocks with zero remaining cycles skipped?
What does a write return, and what happens when all blocks are worn out?
Are there other operations, such as erase or reads?
hints: Keep the writable blocks ordered by (remaining writes, id).
A heap gives the minimum in logarithmic time and handles ties through the id in the key.
After a write only the chosen block changes: decrement it, and remove it when it reaches zero.
invariants: the heap holds exactly the blocks with at least one remaining write
every key is (remaining writes, id)
chooseWhen: Allocation by a priority over mutable counters
tradeoffs: A heap is general and logarithmic; for writes alone the order of blocks never changes, so a pointer would also work

clarifyingQuestions: Are coordinates integers?
Can an attack land partly or wholly outside [0, n]?
Does attacking the same spot twice matter?
hints: With integer coordinates the base is n unit segments.
Only attacks with 0 <= x < n destroy a segment of the base.
Count distinct destroyed segments in a set; the base is gone when the count reaches n, which works even for huge n.
invariants: the counter equals the number of distinct in-range attacked segments
isDestroyed never turns false again once true
tradeoffs: A hash set handles huge n; a bit array is faster for small n but needs n memory
hack2hire:679da470996c3c60bd38b5ba.variantLabel: Single variant: is the whole base covered by unit attacks

constraints: state has only "0" and "1" and at least one "1"
clarifyingQuestions: How many operations are performed, and is m an input?
Can an element be appended more than once?
Do blocked elements unblock to the right, to the left, or both?
hints: Choosing an element never changes which elements become available later.
So S[t] is simply the largest value available at step t.
Availability spreads one index to the right per step from every "1"; compute each index's distance to its nearest "1" on the left and take running maxima.
invariants: the available set only grows
S is non-decreasing
chooseWhen: Greedy choices that do not influence future options
tradeoffs: Distance buckets are linear; a step-by-step simulation is O(n * m)
hack2hire:678876fe402dc47b67a14944.variantLabel: Single variant: lexicographically largest generated array

clarifyingQuestions: How much health does one attack remove, and how many servers can be attacked per round?
Do the requests of the round in which a server falls still count?
Is the answer the requests handled, or the number of attacks?
hints: Splitting hits between servers only delays everything; finish one server before starting another.
Each server is a job with length ceil(health / k) and weight request; the total is the weighted sum of finish times.
Swap two adjacent jobs: i before j is better when t_i * request[j] < t_j * request[i], so sort by that rule (Smith's rule).
invariants: the total equals sum request[i] * (finish round of i)
equal ratios give equal totals in any order
tradeoffs: Cross-multiplied comparison is exact; sorting by a floating ratio could misorder close values
hack2hire:67a56d81b571d6ff0a4bd238.variantLabel: Single variant: order attacks to minimise handled requests

clarifyingQuestions: Are equal values allowed in a triple?
Must the indices be strictly increasing?
How large can the count get?
hints: Fix the middle element of the triple.
The number of triples through j is (larger values left of j) times (smaller values right of j).
Count both with a Fenwick tree over value ranks, one sweep left to right and one right to left.
invariants: equal values are never counted as larger or smaller
each triple is counted once, at its middle index
chooseWhen: Counting monotone patterns of length three
tradeoffs: Fenwick trees are short and exact; merge-sort counting is equivalent but longer
hack2hire:67840e27d0faf7ec64cc3adb.variantLabel: Single variant: count strictly decreasing triples

constraints: userId is 1 to 12 characters from a-z, 0-9 and "_"
orderType is 1 to 12 characters from a-z
amount is a decimal number string
clarifyingQuestions: What do the trust-score methods compute?
Do the two distinct order types have to come from different days?
Is the sort plain string order?
hints: Each query depends only on the logs, so precompute.
Per user keep two day flags and a set of order types.
Select users with both flags and at least two types, sort once, and return a copy each time.
invariants: a user's type set is the union over both days
returned lists are fresh and sorted
chooseWhen: Per-entity aggregation across two data sets
tradeoffs: Precomputing makes repeated calls cheap; rescanning is simpler but O(R) per call
hack2hire:6897c08aa543d38b79706ca6.variantLabel: Single variant: users active on both days with two or more order types

constraints: every intermediate value is at most 2**53 - 1 in absolute value
clarifyingQuestions: Is the syntax prefix "(add 1 2)", function-call "add(1, 2)" or infix?
How many arguments can add and mul take?
Can literals be negative?
hints: Split the input into "(", ")", operation names and literals.
A call needs its operation and a running accumulator; nested calls need a stack of these.
On ")" pop the frame and fold its value into the frame below with that frame's operation; an explicit stack avoids recursion limits on deep nesting.
invariants: the stack holds one frame per open call
each frame's accumulator equals the fold of the arguments closed so far
tradeoffs: An explicit stack handles any depth; recursive descent is shorter but limited by the call stack

input: ( mul ( add ( add 4 2) ( add  0  7  -2 )) (add  ( mul 4 7 -5 )  (add 5 -6)  ( add -1 4)) (add  (add  -1  1  2)  ( add -3 0 -3 )  6 ) )

constraints: userId is 1 to 10 characters from a-z and 0-9
eventType is 1 to 10 characters from a-z and "_"
clarifyingQuestions: What exactly is "frequent": a count threshold, the most frequent type, or per user?
Is the 24-hour window inclusive at the end?
What order should the result use?
hints: Events of different users or types never combine, so group by (user, event).
Within a group sort the timestamps; any window of k consecutive sorted timestamps is the tightest.
A group qualifies when some ts[i + k - 1] - ts[i] < 86400; collect qualifying types in a set and sort it.
invariants: each window covers consecutive sorted timestamps of one group
a type is reported once even if several users qualify
tradeoffs: Sorting per group is simple and exact; a global time-ordered sweep with per-group deques also works for streams
hack2hire:687e65b7eab243475a7dfbf7.variantLabel: Single variant: event types some user repeats k times within 24 hours

constraints: node names are 1 to 5 characters from A-Z
the graph is acyclic with no repeated edges
clarifyingQuestions: Which path is returned when several are longest?
What is returned for an empty edge list?
Is length counted in nodes or edges?
hints: Longest paths in a DAG are a dynamic programme over a topological order.
Compute, for every node, the longest path starting there and its next node.
Breaking ties by the smallest next name gives the lexicographically smallest list, because all candidates start with the same node.
invariants: len[v] = 1 + max len[successor], or 0 for a sink
the chosen continuation of v is lexicographically smallest among longest ones
chooseWhen: Longest or critical path in a dependency graph
tradeoffs: Kahn order avoids deep recursion on long chains; memoised DFS is shorter but recursive
hack2hire:6775decc2c61a9f93e698ba0.variantLabel: Single variant: longest path with a lexicographic tie rule

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer the time, the count, or both?
Which time is returned when the peak is reached several times?
Does a guest leaving at t count at t?
hints: The attendance only rises at entry times, so the peak starts at some entry time.
Sort entries and exits; at equal times process exits first since [entry, exit) is half-open.
Record the time when the running count first beats the best seen.
invariants: the running count equals the guests present just after processing time t
the recorded time only changes on a strict improvement
tradeoffs: Two sorted arrays are simple; a single sorted event list with tie ordering is equivalent
hack2hire:69279ce99c0536c47b291a80.variantLabel: Single variant: earliest moment of peak attendance

clarifyingQuestions: Are substrings counted by position or as distinct strings?
Is y a vowel?
Can a and b be zero or negative?
hints: Write the length as V + C and move everything to one side.
The condition becomes (1 - a) V + (1 - b) C = 0, which is additive over prefixes.
Two prefixes with the same key bound a redundant substring; count pairs of equal keys with a hash map.
invariants: the key of a substring is the difference of two prefix keys
every pair of equal prefix keys is counted once
chooseWhen: Counting substrings by a linear condition on letter classes
tradeoffs: The prefix-key map is linear; the direct check is quadratic but needs no algebra
hack2hire:677041e0366afdc1233e4ff4.variantLabel: Single variant: count substrings with length a * V + b * C

clarifyingQuestions: Is a car counted at its exit timestamp?
Can exit be before entry or beyond n - 1?
Is the output one count per timestamp?
hints: Each ticket adds 1 to a contiguous range of timestamps.
Record the start and end of each range instead of filling it.
Put +1 at entry and -1 at exit + 1 in a difference array; its prefix sums are the counts.
invariants: the prefix sum at t counts tickets with entry <= t <= exit
the difference array sums to zero over 0..n
chooseWhen: Range increments with point reads at the end
tradeoffs: A difference array is linear; per-ticket filling is O(n * tickets) in the worst case
hack2hire:69b78e4e8a0eeb9897a8d2a5.variantLabel: Single variant: occupancy count at every timestamp
